summaries.summary: Propaganda aims to influence people's mindset to advance a specific agenda, and Internet-era social network sharing lets campaigns reach very large audiences.
Propagandist news articles use techniques such as whataboutism, red Herring, and name calling, and fine-grained language analysis can yield more reliable, explainable systems.
The authors organised the NLP4IF@EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019 shared task on a corpus of news articles annotated with 18 propagandist techniques at the fragment level.
Prior propaganda work mostly used article-level labels from distant supervision, including corpora labelled propaganda, trusted, hoax, or satire and binary propagandist vs. non-propagandist articles.
Computational argumentation addresses propaganda-related logical fallacies, including ad hominem corpora and Argotario, whose by-product has $1.3k$ arguments annotated with five fallacies.
Unlike BIBREF8, BIBREF9, BIBREF7, the corpus uses 18 techniques on the same news articles and annotates minimal fragments instead of entire arguments.
The most relevant related work is the authors' parallel EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019 paper BIBREF10, describing a corpus that is a subset of the shared-task corpus.
The shared task uses 18 psychological and rhetorical propaganda techniques found in news articles and intrinsically judgeable without external supporting information.
Loaded language uses words/phrases with strong emotional implications, positive or negative, to influence an audience BIBREF11.
Name calling or labeling labels the propaganda object as something the target audience fears, hates, finds undesirable, loves, or praises BIBREF12.
Repetition repeats the same message over and over again so that the audience will eventually accept it BIBREF13, BIBREF12.
Exaggeration or minimization represents something excessively or makes it seem less important or smaller, e.g., saying that an insult was just a joke.
Doubt questions the credibility of someone or something.
Appeal to fear/prejudice builds support by instilling anxiety and/or panic towards an alternative, possibly based on preconceived judgments.
Flag-waving plays on strong national feeling or group feeling, e.g., race, gender, political preference, to justify or promote an action or idea BIBREF15.
Causal oversimplification assumes one cause when multiple causes exist and includes scapegoating blame transferred to one person or group without investigating complexities.
Slogans are brief, striking phrases that may include labeling and stereotyping and tend to act as emotional appeals BIBREF16.
Appeal to authority states a claim is true because a valid authority/expert supports it without other evidence, including non-authority testimonial references.
Black-and-white fallacy, dictatorship presents two alternatives as the only possibilities, with dictatorship as an extreme case telling the audience exactly what actions to take.
Thought-terminating cliché uses short, generic words or phrases that discourage critical thought and meaningful discussion by offering seemingly simple answers or distracting attention.
Whataboutism discredits an opponent's position by charging hypocrisy without directly disproving their argument BIBREF19.
Reductio ad Hitlerum persuades audiences to disapprove an action or idea by suggesting it is popular with groups hated in contempt by the target audience.
Red herring introduces irrelevant material to divert attention from the points made and lead discussion away from the issue in dispute.
Bandwagon attempts to persuade the target audience to join an action because “everyone else is taking the same action” BIBREF15.
Obfuscation, intentional vagueness, confusion uses deliberately unclear words to let the audience have its own interpretation BIBREF21, BIBREF11.
Straw man substitutes an opponent's proposition with a similar one which is then refuted in place of the original BIBREF22.
The shared task features two subtasks.
Fragment-Level Classification task (FLC) detects all text spans using a propaganda technique in a news article and identifies the technique for each span.
Sentence-Level Classification task (SLC) predicts propaganda or non-propaganda for a sentence, considered propagandist if it contains at least one propagandist fragment.
Both tasks use free-text news articles from 36 propagandist and 12 non-propagandist news outlets, with BIBREF10 describing 450 articles and 47 additional articles annotated.
Training, development, and test partitions contain 350, 61, and 86 articles and 16,965, 2,235, and 3,526 sentences, respectively, with overlapping annotated fragments.
Table TABREF23 reports total instances per technique and percentages of total annotations for the training and development sets.
The shared task had a development phase with labeled training and development datasets and a testing phase with testing input.
Participants tried to achieve the best performance on the development set, and a live leaderboard tracked submissions.
The test set was released, and participants had few days to make final predictions.
In phase 2, no immediate feedback on submissions was provided, and the winner was determined by performance on the test set.
FLC combines propagandist text fragment identification and 18-way technique classification, using modified F$_1$ for partial span matching and per-technique F$_1$ values.
SLC is a binary classification task with imbalanced data, with standard F$_1$ as the official evaluation measure and Precision and Recall also reported.
The SLC baseline is a default-parameter logistic regression classifier using sentence length as its single feature, with performance in Tables TABREF33 and TABREF34.
The FLC baseline generates spans and randomly selects one of the 18 techniques, with its inefficacy illustrated in Tables TABREF36 and TABREF41.
A total of 90 teams registered, 39 submitted 3,065 submissions, with 21 teams making 527 FLC submissions and 35 teams making 2,538 SLC submissions.
The authors overview approaches described in participants' papers, with Tables TABREF28 and TABREF29 offering a high-level summary.
Team newspeak achieved the best FLC test results using 20-way word-level BERT classification, unsupervised fine-tuning on the 1M news dataset and Wikipedia, and oversampling.
Team Stalin used data augmentation and synthetic minority class over-sampling for ELMo, BERT, and Grover contextual embeddings, then fed learned representations into an LSTM.
Team CAUnLP used two context-aware BERT representations with article title and previous sentence, subsampling, and BERT$_{BASE}$ and BERT$_{LARGE}$ experiments.
Team LIACC used hand-crafted features and pre-trained ELMo embeddings, observing a performance boost when balancing the dataset by dropping negative examples.
Team JUSTDeep combined GloVe word embeddings, affection vectors, lexical features, and an ensemble of bi-LSTM, XGBoost, and variations of BERT.
Team YMJA used fine-tuned BERT and created an ensemble of models via cross-validation inspired by kaggle competitions on sentiment analysis.
Team jinfen used logistic regression with TF.IDF and BERT vectors, vocabularies, and readability measures.
Team Tha3aroon implemented an ensemble of three classifiers: two based on BERT and one based on a universal sentence encoder BIBREF36.
Team NSIT explored three popular transfer learning models: various versions of ELMo, BERT, and RoBERTa BIBREF38.
Team Mindcoders combined BERT, Bi-LSTM and Capsule networks BIBREF40 into one deep neural network pre-trained on related-task corpora, e.g., emotion classification.
Team ltuorp used an attention transformer using BERT trained on Wikipedia and BookCorpus.
Team MIC-CIS used a voting ensemble for SLC and an LSTM-CRF multi-task neural sequence tagger for FLC, applying sentence- and fragment-level models jointly.
Team CUNLP used fine-tuned BERT and a logistic regressor with LIWC and punctuation features for SLC, and Bi-LSTM-CRF with character- and word-level embeddings for FLC.
Team ProperGander used BERT with oversampling and cost-sensitive classification for SLC, and a BERT model with Continuous Random Field stacked on an LSTM for FLC.
SLC test results are in Table TABREF33 and development results in Table TABREF34, with decreased F$_1$ values suggesting development-set overfitting.
Tables TABREF36 and TABREF41 report FLC test and development results, which are more stable, with newspeak nearly maintaining its difference from Antiganda.
The NLP4IF@EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019 shared task received 25 SLC and 12 FLC test submissions; SLC was easier, while FLC was more challenging.
The authors plan to make the schema and dataset publicly available beyond NLP4IF and hope the corpus interests Argumentation and Sentiment Analysis researchers.
As an advertisement, Task 11 at SemEval 2020 is a follow up of this shared task and features two complimentary tasks.
Given a free-text article, identify the propagandist text spans.
Given a text span already flagged as propagandist and its context, identify the specific propaganda technique it contains.
This setting would let participants focus on binary sequence labeling for Task 1 and multi-class classification for Task 2.

This research is part of the Propaganda Analysis Project within the Tanbih project, developed by Qatar Computing Research Institute (QCRI), HBKU and MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL).
The corpus for the task was annotated by A Data Pro, a company that performs high-quality manual annotations.
